stem: Which of the following statements about Fragile X syndrome is not correct?
options: It accounts for 10-12% of intellectual disability in males
It is associated with trinucleotide CGG repeats at a fragile site on the Y chromosome
It is associated with mitral valve prolapse
Brain imaging may show reduced posterior cerebellar vermis
correctAnswer: It is associated with trinucleotide CGG repeats at a fragile site on the Y chromosome
explanation: Fragile X syndrome is a common inherited cause of intellectual disability (ID) with X-linked dominant transmission. Penetrance is low, but greater in males than females due to the ‘protective’ effects of the second normal X chromosome in females. Fragile X syndrome accounts  for 10-12% of ID in men. The syndrome is associated with a large sequence of triplet repeats (CGG) at a fragile site on the X chromosome (Xq27.3). The gene sequence is designated FMR-1. Clinical features include a large head, large ears, elongated face, high arched palate, short stature, mitral valve prolapse, poor muscle tone, large testes (macroorchidism), and hyperextensible joints. Brain imaging may show enlarged ventricles, enlarged hippocampus and caudate nuclei, and reduced posterior cerebellar vermis.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 814. Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 86.

stem: Which of the following is correct concerning fragile X syndrome and IQ in males?
options: Length of triplet repeats is inversely related to the IQ
Abstract reasoning abilities are higher than expected during adolescence
IQ stabilises around 20-30 yrs of age
Cognitive degeneration is characteristic of the disease
correctAnswer: Length of triplet repeats is inversely related to the IQ
explanation: The higher the triplets, the lower the IQ. A drop in IQ is noted especially in males with Fragile X. This is most pronounced between ages 8-12 and stabilises by puberty (age 15). No further drop occurs after this, and, in fact, the adaptive skills improve continuously in most males. Hence, FXMR cannot be classed as a degenerative disease. The IQ drop phenomenon may be related to higher stress upon abstract abilities in different IQ tests used for adults and adolescents compared to children. Being concrete thinkers, most FXMR males show a drop in IQ.  This drop is correlated with methylation status of FMR1 gene.

stem: Which of the following is not a feature of Cornelia de Lange syndrome?
explanation: Cornelia de Lange syndrome is a rare genetic disorder associated with a lack of pregnancy-associated plasma protein (PAPPA) linked to chromosome 9q33. A similar phenotype is associated with trisomy 5p, ring chromosome 3. Individuals with Cornelia de Lange syndrome  have severe to profound intellectual disability. Clinical features include short stature, hypertrichosis (hirsutism, synophrys (continuous eyebrows), long eyelashes), prominent philtrum, small upturned nose, thin down-turning upper lip, microcephaly, low-set ears, and small hands and feet. It is also associated with GI problems (in particular reflux), congenital heart defects, visual and hearing problems, skin problems, epilepsy, and death in infancy. Behavioural problems include self-injury, temper tantrums, stereotypic movements, and twirling.

stem: Which of the following features is NOT suggestive of Lennox-Gastaut syndrome?
options: Diffuse interictal slow spike-waves on waking EEG
Most often appears between ages of 3 and 5
explanation: Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (LGS) is a severe form of epilepsy with onset in childhood (age of onset usually before 8 years; peak between 3 and 5 years). The syndrome is defined by a triad of multiple drug-resistant seizure types (tonic, atonic, and atypical absences); a specific EEG  pattern showing burst of slow spike-wave complexes or generalised paroxysmal fast activity; and intellectual disability. The interictal EEG pattern of slow spike-waves is associated with LGS, though not pathognomonic of the disorder. Atonic seizures are common in LGS; they are also known as ‘drop attacks’ or ‘drop seizures’ because they are characterised by a sudden loss of muscle tone that can result in the patient falling to the ground. LGS has deleterious effects on intellectual functioning. Cognitive impairment usually becomes more apparent over time, and within 5 years of onset, serious intellectual problems have developed in most patients.
reference: Asadi-Pooya AA. Lennox-Gastaut syndrome: a comprehensive review. Neurological Sciences. 2018 Mar 1;39(3):403-14. Strzelczyk A, Schubert-Bast S. Expanding the treatment landscape for Lennox-Gastaut syndrome: current and future strategies. CNS drugs. 2021 Jan;35(1):61-83.

stem: Which of the following suggests a 'subcultural' rather than a biological cause for intellectual disability?
options: Equal distribution across families of different types of socio-economic status
Intellectual ability is impaired in family members
Males are more commonly affected than females
correctAnswer: Intellectual ability is impaired in family members
explanation: Although the concept of ‘psychosocial’ causation (due to physical and emotional neglect) for intellectual disability is controversial, mild or borderline intellectual impairment is more common in families of lower socio-economic status (SES). This is best viewed as a cultural norm,  and individuals generally have no, or only minor, impairments in adaptive functioning. Generally, the intellectual ability of family members is also in the borderline range, dysmorphic characteristics are less likely, and other impairments or disabilities are unusual (‘subcultural’ intellectual disability). This is in contrast to biological causation where impairments are more significant, there is no difference in SES, parents and siblings are usually of normal intelligence, and dysmorphic features are more common.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 791.

Common substances include dirt, stones, plastic,  paper, hair, faeces, wood, string, etc. Pics is more frequent in people with intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder.

stem: Which of the following techniques is used to treat stuttering?
explanation: Treatment of stuttering falls into two general categories: indirect and direct. Indirect treatment does not use overt or explicit methods with the child. Rather, it targets parent counselling, and/or the use of the parent/clinician to model fluency facilitators for the child. Direct  treatments usually explicitly teach the child to change something about the way the child speaks. Direct treatments may focus on obtaining ‘smooth speech’ through fluency shaping strategies based on prolonged speech principles that include gradual phonatory initiation, smooth transitions between words using imagery that appeals to children, or stuttering modification. The clinician and/or parent models a slow, relaxed speaking pattern that emphasises reduced rate, smooth articulatory transitions, and slightly prolonged consonants and vowels, while preserving the natural intonation and stress patterns. Shenker RC, Santayana G. What are the options for the treatment of stuttering in preschool children? In Seminars in speech and language 2018 Sep (Vol. 39, No. 04). pp. 313-323.

stem: You are counselling a mother who has one child with autism and is expecting her second. She wishes to know the risk of autism in this second child. The correct answer is
explanation: The risk of autism in a sibling of an autistic child is estimated to be less than 10%, provided only one child in the family has autism so far. correctAnswer: An exaggerated startle response is often seen
explanation: In studies of PTSD in the general adult population with learning disability, the symptoms most commonly reported were nightmares, a feeling of jumpiness and trouble sleeping (Helzer et al. 1987). In half of those with symptoms, the symptoms lasted less than 6 months, but for one-third the symptoms persisted for over a year. It is unusual for PTSD to occur in isolation and comorbidity with other psychiatric disorders is the norm. People with learning disability are at greater risk for the psychiatric disorder than the general population (Rutter at al  1970). Individuals with mild to profound learning disability suffer disorders similar to those affecting the general population. The main difficulty is the diagnosis, as the presentations of a disorder may be different in those with severe developmental delay. Therefore, the diagnosis of PTSD in those who have a severe learning disability, who do not have the communication skills to describe their thoughts, feelings and mood may be hindered. At times we are reliant on observing changes in behaviour and function, for example, aggression, regressive behaviours and changes in sleep pattern. Owing to the limited recognition of PTSD in people with learning disability these symptoms may be attributed to other psychiatric diagnoses. explanation: Although the concept of ‘psychosocial’ causation (due to physical and emotional neglect) for intellectual disability is controversial, mild or borderline intellectual impairment is more common in families of lower socio-economic status (SES). There is a relationship between the length of the DNA trinucleotide repeat and the level of intelligence
correctAnswer: There is a relationship between the length of the DNA trinucleotide repeat and the level of intelligence
explanation: Fragile X syndrome is an X-Linked disorder with an unusual pattern of inheritance. The fragility of the X chromosome is now known to be associated with an unstable region in the fragile-X mental retardation (FMR-1) gene, which was first described in 1991. This region of unstable DNA increases in length and degree of instability in successive generations ( a pre-mutation) until a critical point is reached, and the gene no longer functions (a full mutation). The instability is caused by an increase in CGG repeats from the 50 or so repeats that are usual to  50-100 repeats (pre-mutation) to over 230 repeats (full mutation). The chance of a child inheriting a lengthened gene is proportional to the length of the unstable region in the carrier mother. The severity of the intellectual disability probably depends mostly on the proportion of cells in which the abnormal chromosome is inactivated, X inactivation being random. The associated intellectual disability is mild to moderate. (Ref: New oxford textbook of psychiatry-2nd edition, 1840)

correctAnswer:

She has tumours in the lungs and kidneys → Tuberous sclerosis, A 12-year-old boy with a long face, large ears, enlarged testes and short stature. He also has some speech abnormalities → Fragile X syndrome, A 6-year-old boy with small skull, oblique upward slanted palpebral fissures, protruding tongue, high arched palate and short, broad hands with a single transverse palmar crease → Downs syndrome, A 3- year-old girl achieved normal milestones until the age of 6 months. 1) The description is suggestive of tuberous sclerosis, learning disability of various degrees can present along with intractable seizures, hamartomas of the central nervous system and depigmented skin patches (ash leaf spots) and fibromas of the nails.) 2) Fragile X syndrome is characterized by the presence of a long narrow face, large ears, short stature, macroorchidism (large testicles),  midface hypoplasia, high arched palate, and macrocephaly. Speech abnormalities such as perseveration of words, echolalia, palilalia (repetition of words with increasing speed and decrescendo of volume), cluttering and narrative speech (language that is often devoid of content, yet the language structure remains intact) are reported.

3) Children with Down syndrome show hypotonia, oblique palpebral fissures, abundant neck skin, a small, flattened skull, high cheekbones and a protruding tongue. High-arched palate and a single palmar crease (simian crease) with syndactyly (webbed fingers), and altered dermatoglyphics is also noted. 4) Rett syndrome is seen exclusively in girls. There is normal development up to 6 months. Between 6-18 months, there are subtle developmental deviations. There is a development of abnormal movements like hand flapping and hand wringing, often with autistic features. There is a characteristic progression to severe disability with moderate to severe LD. 5) Rubinstein Taybi syndrome is characterized by short stature, microcephaly, broad thumb, big toes, prominent nose, wide nasal bridge, hypertelorism, beaked nose, long eyelashes, expressive language difficulties, and performance IQ being greater than verbal IQ. People with this syndrome have a friendly disposition, a propensity to self-stimulatory activities such as rocking and do not tolerate of loud noises.

stem:
Treatment methods in learning disability (2) For the following clinical situations, identify the most appropriate treatment from the list:

A 43-year-old man with learning disability is paranoid about nurses on the ward and is seen responding to voices Choose...

A 37-year-old man with learning disability is overactive and has frequent aggressive outbursts on the ward. He has a diagnosis of bipolar disorder Choose...

A 28-year-old woman with Down's syndrome with low mood is isolating herself, doesn't engage in conversations and has poor sleep pattern. Choose...

A 13-year-old boy with Downs' syndrome is reported to be hyperactive, restless and difficult to manage. He has a reduced attention span, and occupational therapist could not engage him in any therapeutic activities. Choose...

An 18-year-old woman with moderate level of learning disability has severe self-injurious behaviour including hand biting and biting off her lips. She does not appear depressed Choose...


correctAnswer:
A 43-year-old man with learning disability is paranoid about nurses on the ward and is seen responding to voices → Risperidone, A 37-year-old man with learning disability is overactive and has frequent aggressive outbursts on the ward. He has a diagnosis of bipolar disorder → Lithium, A 28-year-old woman with Down's syndrome with low mood is isolating herself, doesn't engage in conversations and has poor sleep pattern. → Citalopram, A 13-year-old boy with Downs' syndrome is reported to be hyperactive, restless and difficult to manage. He has a reduced attention span, and occupational therapist could not engage him in any therapeutic activities. → Methylphenidate, An 18-year-old woman with moderate level of learning disability has severe self-injurious behaviour including hand biting and biting off her lips. She does not appear depressed → Naltrexone




explanation:
1) Antipsychotics are used for the treatment of comorbid psychiatric disorders (e.g. schizophrenia and related psychosis) and acute behavioural disturbance. Low dose antipsychotics are also helpful to reduce stereotypies. Both oral and depot neuroleptics are frequently used in treating behavioural and psychiatric symptoms in people with learning disability. Second generation drugs such as risperidone should be tried first. 2) Lithium is useful in the treatment bipolar affective disorder and augmentation of antidepressant therapy and is also helpful in reducing  aggressive outbursts. It is licensed for the 'control of aggressive behaviour or intentional self-harm'. EEG must be obtained as a baseline along with renal functions and cell counts before lithium is started. The therapeutic dose of lithium may induce seizures in those with LD and epilepsy. Patients with pre-existing EEG changes are more prone to lithium toxicity (Frith Prescribing Guidelines p.99).

3) Antidepressants are helpful for the treatment of depression, OCD, self-injurious behaviour and other anxiety disorders. SSRIs such as citalopram should be tried first. 4) This boy is exhibiting features of ADHD. Stimulants such as methylphenidate could be used for the treatment of co-morbid ADHD. 5) Opiate antagonist naltrexone may be effective in the treatment of repetitive self-injury. It may decrease self-injurious behaviour acutely, but it is less effective in the long term.

4) Laurence Moon Biedl syndrome is associated with multiple loci (11q13, 11 q21). In this condition, there is central obesity, polydactyly and mild to moderate LD. Other features include short stature, spastic paraparesis, hypogenitalism, night blindness (due to red cone atrophy), NIDDM, renal problems (diabetes insipidus and kidney failure). (Ref: Oxford handbook- pg 707). 5) In Angelman syndrome, there is deletion in 15q12 of maternal origin; 80% of cases is due to deletion of maternally derived chromosome 15.


explanation:
Explanation:  1) Psychotic disorders, particularly schizophrenia, appear to be more common in those who also have a learning disability. The rate is raised threefold over the general population. Most studies report a prevalence of 3 to 3.5 percent for schizophrenia in learning disabled population. 2) The prevalence of depression is around 2-4%. Depressed mood and vegetative symptoms are the most striking symptoms, even though complaints of depression are not always expressed. A depressive mood is not verbalized, particularly among individuals at a lower intelligence level, but may well be observable. 3) Epilepsy is more prevalent and harder to diagnose and treat in people with mental retardation than in those with normal intellect. Population-based studies have revealed that mental retardation occurs in at least 30 to 40 percent of individuals with epilepsy while the  prevalence of epilepsy in the mentally retarded population is about 20 to 25 percent. It is higher in severe (30-50%) than mild (15-20%) LD. 4) Autistic spectrum disorder and ADHD is increasingly common with increasing severity of LD. It is often a prominent feature in children with LD (up to 20%). Stimulants may help in persons with mild LD with apparent symptoms, but has no clear efficacy in severe-profound LD.

5) The self-injurious behaviour occurs in approximately 20% of adults with learning disability and up to 50% in those requiring institutional care. The self-injurious behaviour occurs more often among persons with moderate and severe mental retardation (IQ < 50). This type of behaviour occurs most frequently between the ages of 10 and 30, with a peak between 15 and 20 years of age.
